section.title: The Law and the Promise
section.sectionRationale: Paul explains how the law relates to the promise given to Abraham. The promise, made to Abraham and to his seed, who is Christ, came first and cannot be annulled by the law that arrived 430 years later. The law was a temporary guardian to lead us to Christ, until faith came. Now all who belong to Christ are one, neither Jew nor Greek, and heirs according to the promise.
section.thesis: The promise God made to Abraham and his seed, who is Christ, precedes and outranks the law, which was added temporarily as a guardian to expose sin and lead us to Christ; now that faith has come, all who are baptized into Christ are one, Abraham's seed, and heirs according to the promise.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the promise to Abraham's seed, who is Christ, cannot be annulled by the later law; the purpose of the law as a temporary guardian until Christ; and the result, that all who belong to Christ are one and are heirs of the promise.

units.label: The promise outranks the law
units.note: to Abraham and to his seed, who is Christ

verses.text: Brothers, let me put this in human terms. Even a human {{diatheke|covenant}}, once it is ratified, cannot be canceled or amended.
The promises were spoken to Abraham and to his {{sperma|seed}}. The Scripture does not say, “and to seeds,” meaning many, but “and to your seed,” meaning One, who is Christ.
What I mean is this: The law that came 430 years later does not revoke the covenant previously established by God, so as to nullify the promise.
For if the inheritance depends on the law, then it no longer depends on a promise; but God freely granted it to Abraham through a promise.
Why then was the law given? It was added because of transgressions, until the arrival of the seed to whom the promise referred. It was administered through angels by a mediator.
A mediator is unnecessary, however, for only one party; but God is one.
Is the law, then, opposed to the promises of God? Certainly not! For if a law had been given that could impart life, then righteousness would certainly have come from the law.
But the Scripture pronounces all things confined by sin, so that by faith in Jesus Christ the promise might be given to those who believe.
Before this faith came, we were held in custody under the law, locked up until faith should be revealed.
So the law became our {{paidagogos|guardian}} to lead us to Christ, that we might be justified by faith.
Now that faith has come, we are no longer under a guardian.

units.label: One in Christ, heirs of the promise
units.note: neither Jew nor Greek, all one

verses.text: You are all sons of God through faith in Christ Jesus.
For all of you who were baptized into Christ have clothed yourselves with Christ.
There is neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free, male nor female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus.
And if you belong to Christ, then you are Abraham's seed and {{kleronomos|heirs}} according to the promise.

diatheke.gloss: A covenant, a settled arrangement or will. Paul argues that even a ratified human covenant cannot be set aside or altered, so how much more the covenant of promise God made with Abraham. The word carries the sense of a binding arrangement established by God, which the later law could not annul or amend.

sperma.gloss: Seed, offspring. The word is collective in form but Paul presses that the promise to Abraham's seed points ultimately to one person, Christ, in whom the many are gathered. The single seed is Christ, and all who belong to Him become Abraham's seed and heirs, so the promise narrows to Christ and then widens to all who are His.

paidagogos.gloss: A guardian, the household servant who supervised and disciplined a child until adulthood. The law played this role, guarding and confining God's people, exposing sin, and leading them toward Christ. It was never the permanent way of salvation but a temporary custodian; now that faith has come, the child has grown and is no longer under the guardian.

kleronomos.gloss: An heir, one who receives an inheritance. Because believers belong to Christ, the true seed of Abraham, they become Abraham's seed and heirs according to the promise. The inheritance is received by promise and faith, not earned by law keeping, and it belongs to all who are in Christ without distinction.

basic.context: Paul answers an obvious question: if salvation is by the promise to Abraham, why did God give the law at all? He shows that the promise came first and cannot be cancelled by the later law. The law had a real but temporary job: to expose sin and act as a guardian leading us to Christ. Now that Christ has come, all who trust Him are one, Abraham's heirs.
basic.hermeneutics: Paul thinks in terms of covenant history: promise first, law added later, Christ the goal. He reads the singular word seed as pointing to Christ. Read the passage as a map of how the law fits into God's plan without ever becoming the way of salvation.
basic.originalLanguages: A ratified diatheke, covenant, cannot be annulled, so the law cannot cancel the promise. The promise was to Abraham's sperma, seed, meaning one, who is Christ. The law was a paidagogos, a guardian, leading us to Christ. And all who belong to Christ are kleronomos, heirs, according to the promise.
basic.typology: Abraham's single seed is fulfilled in Christ, in whom the many become one. The law as guardian pictures the whole era before Christ, a childhood under supervision that gives way to the maturity of faith. Baptism into Christ and being clothed with Him fulfill the longing for a righteousness we could wear rather than earn.
basic.christ: Christ is the seed to whom the promise was made, the goal the law was pointing toward, and the one into whom believers are baptized and with whom they are clothed. In Him the distinctions that once divided people fall away, and all become one. He is the heir, and all who belong to Him share the inheritance.
basic.god: God is the promise maker who freely grants the inheritance to Abraham and keeps His word across the centuries. He is one, and His plan is one, moving from promise through law to Christ. He makes sons of God through faith and gathers a single family from every kind of person.
basic.crossReferences: Genesis 12 and 15 record the promise to Abraham. Romans 4 shows the promise came by faith, not law. Colossians 3 says there is no Greek or Jew, for Christ is all and in all.
basic.oneStory: The promise to Abraham is the spine of the biblical story, and here Paul shows how it holds together with the law. The law served for a season, but the promise always aimed at Christ, the seed. In Him a united family of heirs, from every nation, receives what God pledged long ago.

context.literary:
The passage is built around two questions that Paul expects his readers to ask, and the answer to each opens a new movement. After a quick argument from everyday life in verses 15 to 18, he asks in verse 19, 'Why then was the law given?' and answers in verses 19 to 25. In verse 21 he asks, 'Is the law, then, opposed to the promises of God?' and answers with his emphatic 'Certainly not!' The last movement, verses 26 to 29, is not a question but a declaration, and it is the goal toward which the rest has been moving.

The rhythm of the middle section is carried by temporal markers. The law came '430 years later' in verse 17. It was added 'until the arrival of the seed' in verse 19. 'Before this faith came' in verse 23 is answered by 'Now that faith has come' in verse 25. Paul is telling a story in time, with a before and an after, and the law has a definite place in that story. The verbs of confinement multiply in verses 22 and 23, so that the law is seen first as a prison guard and then as a household custodian, which gives two pictures of one reality.

The final unit gathers its weight through repetition. 'All' appears in verses 26, 27 and 28, 'you are all sons,' 'all of you who were baptized,' 'you are all one,' and the phrase 'in Christ' or 'into Christ' runs through the verses as well. The seed of verse 16 returns in verse 29, so that the unit is wrapped by an inclusio around the word 'seed': Christ is the seed in verse 16, and those who belong to Christ are the seed in verse 29. The movement is from the One to the many, and it is stated in those two verses before it is explained.
context.historical:
Paul begins with an analogy from ordinary life, which for his readers would have been as familiar as a will or a contract. The Greek word diatheke could mean a will or testament as well as a covenant, and in either sense it could not simply be set aside once it had been properly ratified. Hebrews 9:15-17 plays on the same double meaning. The Galatians, many of them from Greek-speaking cities, would have understood that a binding agreement could not be changed by a later party.

The number 430 in verse 17 comes from Exodus 12:40-41, where the people of Israel are said to have lived in Egypt for 430 years. The Hebrew text puts the 430 years in Egypt alone, while the Greek translation includes the time in Canaan, which fits Paul's count from Abraham's promise to the giving of the law. Paul does not need to settle the chronology. His point is only that a long interval separated promise and law, so the later could not overrule the earlier.

The 'guardian' of verse 24 is the paidagogos, a figure from the Greco-Roman household. He was typically a trusted slave who took a boy to and from school and watched over his conduct, with the authority to discipline him. He was not the teacher. The image would have been immediately clear: a child under a custodian is protected and restrained, but the arrangement ends when the child comes of age.

The mention of angels in verse 19 reflects a Jewish tradition, found also in Acts 7:53 and Hebrews 2:2, that the law was given with angelic attendance at Sinai. The mediator is Moses. Verse 28 would have been startling in a world where the divisions of Jew and Greek, slave and free, and men and women structured law, worship and daily life. The Jewish morning prayer later recorded in rabbinic sources thanks God for not making the speaker a Gentile, a slave or a woman, and many scholars see Paul answering such a pattern here, though the exact form of the prayer in his day cannot be proved.
context.canonical:
The promise that Paul has in view comes from the stories of Abraham. God said 'to your offspring I will give this land,' Genesis 12:7, repeated in Genesis 13:15, and the promise of a blessing to all nations in Genesis 22:18 follows the offering of Isaac. The covenant is called 'everlasting' in Genesis 17:7-8. Paul's reasoning in Galatians 3:16 thus draws on actual wording in Genesis. The word 'offspring' is a singular collective in Hebrew, and the New Testament sees in it a line running from Abraham through Isaac and David to the Messiah, 2 Samuel 7:12 and Isaiah 53:10.

On the law, Paul's account fits with his teaching elsewhere. Romans 5:20 says the law came in to increase the trespass, and Romans 7:7-12 explains that it was holy and good but made sin known. Colossians 2:16-17 and Hebrews 10:1 speak of the law as a shadow of good things to come. Matthew 5:17 shows Jesus saying He came to fulfil it, not to abolish it. Paul does not belittle the law; he places it in its time.

The pronouncement of verse 28 has strong links to other letters. 1 Corinthians 12:13 says that in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body, whether Jews or Greeks, slaves or free. Colossians 3:9-11 speaks of the new self in which there is no Greek or Jew. The mention of 'male and female' echoes Genesis 1:27, so that Paul seems to say that the creation of humanity in God's image is now renewed in Christ. The inheritance language of verse 29 points forward to Galatians 4:7 and Romans 8:17, and to Revelation 21:7, where the one who conquers inherits all things.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul is answering a charge that he knows is coming, that his gospel makes the law pointless. His reply is neither to dismiss the law nor to make it a second route to God. He wants the Galatians to see the law in its proper place in a story, as something added for a purpose and limited by a time, while the promise stood first and stands last. His practical aim is to take away the force of the rival teachers' argument that the law is the permanent mark of God's people.

He also wants them to take in the cost of misplacing the law. If the inheritance came by law, he says in verse 18, it would not come by promise, and since it did come by promise, a return to law is a return to a different kind of arrangement. The law could not give life, and it was never meant to. Its work was to confine all under sin so that the promise might be given to those who believe.

The final verses are meant to be heard with joy. Paul wants the Galatians to know who they are: sons of God, clothed with Christ, one body, and heirs. This is exactly what the rival teachers were taking from them by suggesting that they needed circumcision to belong. He wants the Gentile believers to leave the argument with a settled identity, and he wants the Jewish believers to see that their own privileges are not lost but fulfilled in a larger family. Verse 28 is not a political programme but a statement about how people stand before God and in the church.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The picture of the law as a guardian is Paul's description of a stage in God's dealings with His people, and it is not a rule for how believers should now treat the Old Testament. The law remains Scripture, and Paul says elsewhere that all of it is useful, 2 Timothy 3:16. What has changed is its standing: it no longer holds believers in custody. That is a description of the epochs, and its application today is that we read the law as pointing to Christ and not as the ground of our acceptance.

The unity of verse 28 is both description and prescription. It describes what God has done: in Christ the barriers have been removed as the ground of standing before God. It also implies a task. If Jew and Gentile, slave and free are one, the church should not allow social divisions to rank its members, which is the point of Paul's rebuke at Antioch and his letter to Philemon. How the verse applies to every question of roles in church and home is debated, and the passage itself does not take that up.

The baptism of verse 27 is described as the moment of clothing with Christ. The passage is not setting out a theory of the sacrament, and readers differ about how to relate baptism and faith, but it is clear that the verse speaks of the union that belongs to every believer. The inheritance of verse 29 is described as a present possession and as a future one, and the New Testament holds both together.

debates.question: How can Paul build an argument on the singular 'seed' in verse 16?

views.label: A grammatical point about the singular
views.case: Paul says that Scripture does not say 'seeds,' meaning many, but 'seed,' meaning one. The word was used for a line of descendants, and in the Genesis promises it often has a collective sense. Paul reads the singular as pointing to Christ in particular, a method of close reading common in his day. The conclusion in verse 29, that those who belong to Christ are Abraham's seed, shows the many are included in the One.

views.label: A corporate seed with Christ as its head
views.case: Others say Paul is not denying the collective sense, since verse 29 uses it himself. He is saying that the promise has one ultimate recipient, in whom the many are included. Christ is the true Israel and the representative of the family. On this reading the argument is about headship, not grammar.

debates.bearing: Both views end in the same place. The promise is fulfilled in Christ, and believers share in it by being in Him, so that the blessing never reaches them apart from Him.

debates.question: What does 'a mediator is unnecessary for only one party; but God is one' mean in verse 20?

views.label: The promise is God's alone, the law involved two parties
views.case: A mediator stands between two parties. The law at Sinai had Moses between God and the people and called for the people's pledge, Exodus 19:8, whereas the promise to Abraham was spoken by God alone and rested on His word. This makes the promise the surer arrangement.

views.label: The law came at a distance, through angels and a mediator
views.case: Others stress verse 19, in which the law came 'through angels by a mediator.' The chain of intermediaries is contrasted with God speaking directly to Abraham. The point is the greater directness of the promise.

debates.bearing: The verse is short and difficult, and wise readers hold their reading lightly. Both views support Paul's main conclusion that the promise is prior and secure, resting on God Himself.

debates.question: What does 'neither male nor female' in verse 28 imply for roles in the church?

views.label: It speaks of equal standing, with no consequences for roles
views.case: Verse 28 sits in a passage on sonship and inheritance, and in both cases the subject is standing before God. Some argue that it says nothing about who may teach or lead, noting that Paul gives role instructions elsewhere, as in 1 Corinthians 14:34-35 and 1 Timothy 2:11-14.

views.label: It undermines every ranking in the church
views.case: Others hold that the verse is the charter of the new community and that its principle should shape all its life. They point to women who served as co-workers in Paul's letters, as in Romans 16:1-7 and Philippians 4:2-3.

debates.bearing: All agree that men and women are equally sons and heirs and that no one is closer to God by sex, status or ancestry. The remaining dispute is over how far the verse carries into the structures of church life, and honest readers will weigh the other passages too.

study.originalLanguages:
The legal vocabulary of verse 15 and 17 is striking. The verb for 'ratified' is kyroo, to make valid or confirm, and its opposite, akyroo, 'nullify' or 'revoke,' occurs in verse 17. Paul adds epidiatassomai, 'amend,' a rare word made from the verbs for 'add' and 'arrange,' for a codicil attached to a will. So the claim is that no one, once an agreement is ratified, may cancel it or attach new conditions. The law that came later cannot be used as a condition on a promise already made.

In verse 18, the verb 'freely granted' is kecharistai, from charizomai, to give as a gift of grace, and it is in the perfect tense. The perfect carries the sense of a completed act with a continuing result: God gave the inheritance to Abraham and it stands as given. The relation between the root of this verb and the noun charis, grace, is plain, and Paul wants the sense of unearned gift to be heard.

Verses 22 and 23 pile up verbs of confinement. 'Confined' in verse 22 is synkleio, to shut up together, the verb used of fish enclosed in a net in Luke 5:6. The 'held in custody' of verse 23 is phroureo, a military term for standing guard, and 'locked up' returns to synkleio. In Romans 11:32 Paul uses the same verb of God's shutting up all in disobedience so as to show mercy. Here sin is the jailer, and the law is the means by which the prisoners are made aware of it. The purpose clause, 'so that the promise might be given,' shows that the confinement serves mercy.

The little phrase eis Christon occurs in verses 24 and 27. In verse 24 the law was a paidagogos 'to lead us to Christ,' and the preposition can mean 'until' or 'unto'; in verse 27 believers were baptized 'into Christ.' The repetition lets Paul's movement of thought be heard: the law's custody led towards Christ, and the baptism takes the believer into Him. The verb enduo, 'clothed yourselves,' in verse 27 is in the middle voice, 'you have put on Christ as a garment,' and the image is taken up in Romans 13:14.

Verse 28 has a small grammatical shift of great interest. The first two pairs, Jew nor Greek, slave nor free, use the word 'nor,' but the third reads 'male and female,' using the words arsen and thelu, which echo the Greek text of Genesis 1:27. And Paul says 'you are all one,' with the word for one in the masculine, heis, so that the unity is of persons in a single body, not of a thing.

typology.fulfillment: God told Abraham that through Isaac his offspring would be named, and Isaac was born by promise, not by natural strength. Romans 9:7-8 draws the lesson that the children of promise are counted as offspring. The correspondence is that of a gift born against expectation. In Christ the promised seed comes at last, and those who are His share the name. The type falls short because Isaac was a single son who could not save, whereas Christ is the Son who saves all who belong to Him, as Galatians 3:29 says.

typology.type: The law as a shadow, Hebrews 10:1
typology.fulfillment: The sacrifices and festivals of the law are described in the New Testament as a shadow of good things to come, Colossians 2:16-17. The guardian of Galatians 3 is the same idea told in the language of a household. The sacrifices repeated year by year could not take away sin, Hebrews 10:1-4, but they taught a people what sin cost and what a substitute might be. Christ is the substance that casts the shadow. The type falls short because a shadow can instruct but cannot cleanse.

The high priest Joshua stands in filthy clothes before the angel of the LORD, and the clothes are removed and clean ones given. Isaiah 61:10 speaks of being clothed with garments of salvation. Paul takes the image for the believer's union with Christ, 'clothed yourselves with Christ.' The escalation is that the garment is not a change of outfit but the person of Christ Himself. The type is incomplete in that Joshua was clothed for a priestly office, while believers are clothed for sonship.

At Babel the human family was scattered into languages and peoples, Genesis 11:7-9. At Pentecost, Acts 2:5-11, the gospel was heard in the languages of many nations. Galatians 3:28 states the result: the divisions are not the final word in Christ. The correspondence is of scattering and gathering. The type is still unfolding, since Revelation 7:9 shows the finished gathering, and the distinctions of nations remain in glory without any longer dividing.

study.christ:
Christ stands at the beginning, middle and end of this passage. In verse 16 He is the seed to whom the promise was made, so that the promise was always pointed at a person. It is not a heap of blessings but a single gift with a single recipient, and the many receive it only as they are joined to Him. That explains why Paul can later say that those who belong to Christ are Abraham's seed, verse 29. The line from Genesis runs through a long history to one man, and in Him it opens again to many.

He is also the end of the law's custody. The law was added 'until the arrival of the seed,' and when Christ came the age of the guardian closed. Paul does not say that Christ makes the law irrelevant; he says that the law was guiding people to Him. Jesus says as much in John 5:39-40, where the Scriptures bear witness to Him, and in Luke 24:44, where everything written about Him in the law, the prophets and the psalms must be fulfilled. The law's demands are met in Him, and its penalties are borne by Him.

In verses 26 to 29 He is the one into whom believers are baptized and with whom they are clothed. The phrase 'in Christ Jesus' carries the whole weight of the paragraph. It is by being in Him that Jew and Gentile are one, and not by a programme of tolerance. In Colossians 3:11 Paul says that Christ is all and in all, and here the same truth is stated: the unity is a person, not a policy. And as the heir of all things, Hebrews 1:2, He shares what is His. The believer is not an heir on his own account but as one joined to the Heir.

The guard against forced allegory here is the fact that Paul himself bases the point on the actual wording of Genesis and gives the reason for his reading. He does not say that every promise in the Old Testament hides a private message about Christ. He says that the promises made to Abraham, as the line of Scripture develops, come to rest on Jesus. A reader who follows Paul will look for the way each Old Testament text belongs to this story and will not invent connections the text does not support.
study.god:
The God of this passage is a promise-maker whose word stands. Paul's argument from the ratified covenant is that if even a human agreement cannot be cancelled, God's own pledge cannot be cancelled by a later arrangement. The point reaches into worship and prayer: we can trust the promises of God because they do not depend on our performance, and they were made before we had done anything. The verb of verse 18, in the perfect tense, says that He has given the inheritance and it stands given.

He is also a God who works through time and in order. The law was not a mistake or a rival plan. It was added at the right moment, for a purpose, and it ended at the right moment. 'Is the law, then, opposed to the promises of God? Certainly not!' The unity of God's purposes is assumed throughout, and the passage helps readers who struggle to see how the Old Testament and the New fit together. The same God is behind the promise, the law and the fulfilment, and His plan has one centre.

The statement that God is one, verse 20, is Paul's compressed reminder of the Shema, Deuteronomy 6:4. The one God is not divided in purpose, and the promise rests on Him alone. In the verses that follow it is the one God who makes all believers one family. Because there is one God over all, there can be one people of God, and the old dividing lines cannot be kept without denying who He is, as Romans 3:29-30 argues.

Finally, God is the Father who makes sons. Verse 26 says that all are 'sons of God through faith,' and verse 29 says they are heirs. The language of family is the language of grace. A guardian restrains, but a father gives an inheritance. The God of Galatians 3 does both in order: He holds His people in custody until the time is ripe, and then He receives them as sons. For worship this means that we approach Him as children, with confidence, and not as prisoners waiting for release.

crossReferences.note: The promise of the land to Abraham's offspring, with the word that Paul reads in Galatians 3:16. Genesis 13:15 repeats it, so the singular offspring is part of the original wording of the promise and not Paul's invention.
After Abraham offered Isaac, God repeated that in his offspring all the nations of the earth would be blessed. It shows that the promise to the nations and the line of the seed belong together.

The 430 years of Israel's sojourn, which Paul uses as the interval between promise and law. The Hebrew and Greek texts reckon the figure a little differently, and Paul's count follows the longer sojourn.
Stephen says the people received the law as ordained by angels and did not keep it. It supports Paul's mention of angels in Galatians 3:19 and shows the idea was familiar in the early church.

The promise to Abraham did not come through the law but through the righteousness of faith, so that it would rest on grace and be guaranteed to all his offspring. It is a close parallel to Galatians 3:17-18.

The law came in so that the trespass might increase. It helps explain 'added because of transgressions' in Galatians 3:19, with the law bringing sin into the light and so preparing the way for grace to abound all the more.
Paul says the law is holy, righteous and good, yet it showed him his sin. It answers the question whether the law is opposed to the promises, as Galatians 3:21 does.

In one Spirit all were baptized into one body, Jews or Greeks, slaves or free. It matches Galatians 3:27-28 and shows that the unity belongs to the Spirit's work and is shared by every believer alike.

The new self is renewed in the image of its Creator, where there is no Greek or Jew, and Christ is all and in all. It is a close parallel to Galatians 3:28, with the creation language of Genesis in the background.
Paul tells believers to put on the Lord Jesus Christ. The same verb as in Galatians 3:27, used here as a daily call, so that what is true in baptism is to be lived.
A will takes effect only when the one who made it has died, and Christ is the mediator of a new covenant. It plays on the same double meaning of diatheke as Galatians 3:15.
God created man in His own image, male and female He created them. The Greek of this verse is echoed in Galatians 3:28, so that the new unity in Christ is the renewal of the creation of humanity.
Jesus did not come to abolish the Law or the Prophets but to fulfil them. It supports Paul's claim that the law is not opposed to God's promises but has its goal in Christ.

study.oneStory:
The promise to Abraham is the thread that runs through the whole Bible, and this passage shows how the law fits into it without breaking it. After the fall in Genesis 3 there is a promise of a seed who will crush the serpent. After the flood and Babel, God calls Abraham and promises a seed through whom the nations will be blessed. Every later development, the exodus, the covenant at Sinai, the kingdom of David, is a step on that road. Paul says that the law was one of these steps, added because of transgressions, until the seed should come.

The picture of custody and guardian helps to see why the story has the shape it does. Israel was like a child heir, protected and corrected, waiting for the time set by the Father. The law kept the line of promise intact, exposed sin so that no one could mistake it, and taught the people what a holy God requires. It also kept alive the longing that something more would come. When Christ arrived, the story turned: the guardian's task was done, and the heir came into his inheritance.

What the passage sets up is the next chapter, in which the heir is shown to be like a child who is no better than a slave until the time appointed, and then God sends His Son and the Spirit. It also sets up the whole of the church's life, a family from all nations in which no one is first by birth. The unity of verse 28 is the reversal of Babel and the beginning of the gathering that the prophets had expected.

The story ends in the new creation with the heirs in possession. Revelation 21:7 says that the one who conquers will inherit all things, and Revelation 7:9 shows the great multitude from every nation. The promise made to one man in Ur has become a promise kept for a countless family. The distinctions of earth are not erased but are no longer barriers, and all stand together in the One who is Abraham's seed and their Lord.

sermon.title: Promise and Law (Galatians 3:15 to 29)
sermon.why: Begg explains how the promise to Abraham relates to the law given later, why the law served as a temporary guardian leading to Christ, and how all who belong to Christ become one and heirs according to the promise.

quiz.q: Why can the law not cancel the promise to Abraham?

options.text: The promise came first and a ratified covenant cannot be annulled by a later law.
options.note: Verses 15 to 17 argue from the priority of the promise.

options.text: Because the law was never really from God.
options.note: The law was from God, but it does not revoke the earlier promise.

options.text: Because Abraham kept the law perfectly.
options.note: The promise rested on God's grace, not Abraham's law keeping.

options.text: Because the promise was only a suggestion.
options.note: It was a binding covenant God freely granted.

quiz.q: Who is the seed to whom the promises were made?

options.text: Christ, in whom all who believe are gathered.
options.note: Verse 16 identifies the one seed as Christ.

options.text: The whole nation of Israel only.
options.note: Paul narrows the seed to one, Christ, then widens it to all who are His.

options.text: Isaac alone.
options.note: Isaac was part of the line, but the promise points ultimately to Christ.

options.text: The angels who administered the law.
options.note: The seed is Christ, not the angels.

quiz.q: What was the purpose of the law?

options.text: A temporary guardian to expose sin and lead us to Christ.
options.note: Verses 19 to 24 describe the law's preparatory role.

options.text: The permanent way to earn righteousness.
options.note: The law could not impart life or justify; it pointed to Christ.

options.text: A means to divide people forever.
options.note: Its role was preparatory, ending in Christ who unites.

options.text: An accident that God later regretted.
options.note: God gave the law with real purpose, until Christ came.

quiz.q: What does verse 28 declare about believers in Christ?

options.text: There is neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free, male nor female; all are one in Christ.
options.note: All share the same standing as sons and heirs.

options.text: Only Jewish believers are truly full members.
options.note: The verse abolishes that ranking; all are one in Christ.

options.text: Believers must erase every created difference.
options.note: The point is equal standing before God, not erasing all distinctions.

options.text: Social status still determines nearness to God.
options.note: All are one in Christ, regardless of status.

quiz.q: What is true of all who belong to Christ?

options.text: They are Abraham's seed and heirs according to the promise.
options.note: Verse 29 grounds every believer in the promise to Abraham.

options.text: They must still earn the inheritance by works.
options.note: The inheritance comes by promise and faith, not works.

options.text: They inherit only if they are physically Jewish.
options.note: Belonging to Christ, not physical descent, makes one an heir.

options.text: They receive nothing until the law is fully kept.
options.note: The inheritance is granted through the promise, received by faith.

questions: God kept His promise to Abraham across centuries and would not let the law overturn it. How does God's covenant faithfulness strengthen your trust in His promises to you?
The law served as a guardian to lead us to Christ. How has a sense of your own failure under God's standard driven you toward Christ rather than away from Him?
In Christ there is neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free, male nor female. Where do you still rank people, and how does your shared standing in Christ challenge that?
Believers are clothed with Christ. What does it mean for God to see you dressed in Christ's righteousness rather than your own record?
You are Abraham's heir according to the promise. How would living as a secure heir, rather than an anxious earner, change your week?

translationNotes.note: Seed renders sperma, collective in form; Paul presses its singular reference to point to one, Christ, in whom the many are gathered as Abraham's offspring.
Guardian translates paidagogos, the household servant who supervised a child to maturity; the term stresses custody and discipline, not classroom instruction.
Administered through angels by a mediator refers to the giving of the law at Sinai through Moses; the point is the law's mediated, secondary character next to the direct promise.

meta.notes: BSB text fetched from bible.helloao.org for Galatians 3:15-29. Sermon verified this session from the Truth For Life series A Study in Galatians, Volume 1 by Alistair Begg.
